conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is false, stating there is no reliable clinical evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19. Therefore, it clearly rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: False.** There is no reliable clinical evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19.

The central problem is that a plausible laboratory property is not proof of a treatment in people. Garlic has antimicrobial compounds, but the WHO states that, despite such properties, **there is no evidence that garlic can prevent COVID-19**—and prevention evidence would not establish the much stronger claim that it can *cure* an active infection. https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/searo/thailand/khai-hua-ror-knowcovid-12-mythd-about-covid-19.pdf

The most directly relevant fact-check evidence reports that a study of garlic reduced viral infectiousness **in test tubes**, not in patients, and that earlier clinical trials found garlic did not improve recovery in COVID-19 patients. Test-tube findings cannot show that boiled garlic water reaches an effective dose, is safe at that dose, or improves outcomes such as symptoms, hospitalization, or death. https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/garlic-covid-cure-claim-crushed-by-experts/

There has been at least one phase-II trial of a *traditional Vietnamese medicine containing garlic extract* for non-severe COVID-19. But that is a manufactured multi-ingredient capsule, not boiled garlic water, and its existence does not validate a cure claim. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37637574/

Do not substitute garlic water for evidence-based medical care. Garlic can cause abdominal symptoms, nausea, allergy, and—in supplement form—may raise bleeding risk. https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/garlic
